title: Preface
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K cover page identifies its fiscal year ended September 28, 2024, California incorporation, headquarters, contact details, and SEC file number. It lists common stock and notes registered on Nasdaq, with no Section 12(g) securities. The filing confirms Apple’s reporting and electronic filing compliance, large accelerated filer status, and auditor attestation of internal controls; it is not a shell company. It reports no indicated financial-statement error correction or restatement-related recovery analysis, approximately $2.629 trillion in nonaffiliate market value, and 15.116 billion shares outstanding as of October 18, 2024.

title: DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
summary: Apple’s 2024 Form 10-K covers the fiscal year ended September 28, 2024, and incorporates portions of its 2025 proxy statement into Part III. It outlines the report’s sections and items across four parts, explains forward-looking-statement risks and terminology, defines fiscal-period references and “Company”/“Apple,” and describes Apple’s business, fiscal year, and product lines: iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, home devices, and accessories.

title: Apple Background, Products, and Forward-Looking Statements
summary: Apple’s 2024 Form 10-K explains that forward-looking statements involve risks, are not guarantees, and may differ from actual results; it identifies common indicators, refers readers to risk factors, and disclaims updates except as required by law. The report uses Apple’s September-ending fiscal calendar and defines Apple as the company and its wholly owned subsidiaries. Apple designs, manufactures, and markets devices and services; its products include iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, home devices, and accessories, with their operating systems and principal product lines described.

title: Services, Segments, and Distribution
key_items: Advertising; AppleCare; Cloud Services; Digital Content; Payment Services
summary: Describes advertising, AppleCare support and protection, cloud services, digital content platforms and subscriptions, and payment services. The business is managed across five geographic segments, defined by region and tailored to local markets. Customers span consumer, business, education, enterprise, and government markets; sales use direct channels (retail and online stores and sales teams) and indirect channels (carriers, wholesalers, retailers, and resellers), accounting for 38% and 62% of 2024 net sales, respectively.

title: Competition
summary: The text outlines Apple’s intense competition, driven by pricing pressure, rapid innovation and imitation, and its dependence on timely product development and factors such as quality, design, ecosystem, distribution and support. It describes competitors’ scale, pricing and free-content strategies. Component supply risks include limited sources, shortages, price swings, custom-part capacity constraints and uncertain supply agreements. Apple relies on R&D, licensing and acquisitions to sustain innovation. It protects a broad global IP portfolio but also depends on third-party rights whose future licensing is not guaranteed.

title: Competition, Supply, R&D and Intellectual Property
summary: The Company’s success depends on innovative products and technologies, and competition spans its devices and services, driven by pricing, features, quality, ecosystems and distribution; rivals may have broader offerings, lower prices, imitate features or use free-content models. Component supply is generally multi-sourced but some parts are limited or custom-sourced, exposing the Company to shortages, price swings, capacity constraints and uncertain supply agreements. R&D, licensing and acquisitions support ongoing innovation. The Company protects innovations through a broad global IP portfolio and applications, but also relies on its personnel and third-party licenses, whose future availability and terms are not guaranteed.

title: Business Seasonality and Human Capital
key_items: Compensation and Benefits; Growth and Development; Workplace Practices and Policies; Inclusion and Diversity; Engagement; Health and Safety
summary: The page explains seasonal sales patterns and how product launches affect sales, costs, and channel inventory. It describes the company’s workforce and its efforts on competitive compensation, benefits, employee development, inclusive and nondiscriminatory workplace practices, diversity and equitable opportunity, employee feedback and engagement, and workplace safety, security, and risk management.

title: Investor Information and Risk Factors
summary: The Company’s SEC filings are available free through its investor relations website, which, along with its corporate website, also provides investor, financial, ESG, and annual-meeting information; website content is not incorporated into the filing, and URLs are textual references only. Risk factors, whether known or unknown, may materially harm the Company’s business, reputation, results, financial condition, or stock price. Past performance is not a reliable guide to future results, and the risk discussion contains forward-looking statements and should be read with the cited MD&A and financial statements.

title: Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

nodes.title: The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.
nodes.summary: Apple’s performance is highly dependent on global and regional economic conditions because most sales and many supplier facilities are outside the U.S. Slow growth, recession, unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency shifts, policy changes, market volatility, and declining incomes or asset values may weaken consumer confidence and demand. Economic uncertainty can also destabilize suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, channel partners, and developers, potentially restricting credit or causing insolvency. Further risks include higher receivables losses, financial counterparty failures, difficulty issuing debt, reduced liquidity, and lower financial-instrument values, potentially harming Apple’s business, results, financial condition, and stock price.

nodes.title: The Company’s business can be impacted by political events, trade and other international disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues, industrial accidents and other business interruptions.
nodes.summary: The Company’s global business, sales, and largely outsourced manufacturing are exposed to political and trade disputes, geopolitical conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, climate-related extreme weather, industrial accidents, cyberattacks, labor disputes, public health emergencies, and other interruptions. Trade restrictions can raise costs and force disruptive, expensive supply-chain or product changes, sometimes with little warning; escalating disputes could worsen impacts. Disruptions may impede manufacturing and delivery, interrupt services and sales, increase costs, and weaken demand. Supplier accidents can cause injuries, deaths, business disruption, and reputational harm; pandemics can additionally constrain travel and freight and delay products and services. Recovery may take substantial time and expense and cause lost sales, especially given reliance on limited component sources; insurance may not cover all losses.

nodes.title: Global markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and subject to rapid technological change, and the Company may be unable to compete effectively in these markets.
nodes.summary: The Company faces intense global competition, rapid technological change, price pressure, short product cycles, evolving standards, and price-sensitive customers. Its success depends on timely innovation and substantial R&D investment, which may not yield returns. Competitors may imitate products or infringe intellectual property, while protections vary by country. The Company has minority shares in smartphone, PC, and tablet markets and competes with better-resourced rivals offering broader, cheaper products, larger device bases, and sometimes loss-making prices; some markets stagnate or contract. Imitation, collaboration, and integrated offerings may intensify competition. Services also compete with established providers, free-content models, and illegitimate content access. Failure to sustain product and service advantages could materially harm its competitive position, business, results, and financial condition.

summary: The section covers risks from adverse global and regional economic conditions, including weakened demand, supplier and partner instability, credit and liquidity constraints, counterparty failures, and financial-market losses. It also addresses disruption from political and trade disputes, geopolitical conflict, terrorism, disasters, climate events, accidents, cyberattacks, labor disputes, and public health emergencies, which can disrupt supply, sales, and services, raise costs, and cause uncovered losses. Finally, it describes intense competition, rapid technological change, price pressure, intellectual-property challenges, and the need for successful innovation to maintain advantages in products and services.

title: Business Risks

nodes.title: To remain competitive and stimulate customer demand, the Company must successfully manage frequent introductions and transitions of products and services.
nodes.summary: Apple’s competitiveness depends on continually introducing and transitioning products, services, and technologies, improving existing offerings, and generating customer demand. Success depends on timely development and market acceptance; managing new-technology and production ramp-up risks; third-party software and support; aligning purchase commitments, inventory, product quantities, and costs with demand; and avoiding defects. New offerings may displace existing ones while generating lower revenue or margins, materially harming business, operating results, and financial condition. Success in future introductions and transitions is not assured.

nodes.title: Manufacturing, Logistics, and Component Supply Risks
key_items: The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on concentrated outsourcing partners, mainly abroad, for manufacturing, assembly, and logistics, reducing control and exposing it to quality, compliance, disruption, warranty, and financial-recovery risks. Supply-chain changes require time and resources. Dependence on single-source suppliers and custom components creates shortages, price volatility, capacity, renewal, and supplier-failure risks; delays or inability to find alternatives can materially harm operations and financial results.

nodes.title: Product Quality, Asset and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: The Company’s products and services may be affected from time to time by design and manufacturing defects that could materially adversely affect the Company’s business and result in harm to the Company’s reputation.
The Company is exposed to the risk of write-downs on the value of its inventory and other assets, in addition to purchase commitment cancellation risk.
The Company relies on access to third-party intellectual property, which may not be available to the Company on commercially reasonable terms, or at all.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from defects in hardware, software, components and services—including outages, safety and security issues, liability, recalls, costs, and reputational or sales harm. It covers inventory obsolescence, asset impairments, cancellation fees, and inaccurate forecasts or unused purchase commitments amid volatile markets. It also explains reliance on third-party intellectual property licenses, potential infringement, and the business impact if rights cannot be obtained on reasonable terms.

nodes.title: Risks to Software and Digital Content
key_items: The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers.

Failure to obtain or create digital content that appeals to the Company’s customers, or to make such content available on commercially reasonable terms, could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.
nodes.summary: The Company’s product demand depends on third-party developers creating and maintaining compelling applications; its smaller market share may steer developers toward competing platforms, and failure to keep pace with technology can harm app quality and customer demand. App Store commissions and sales may be affected by business, legal, competitive, and regulatory changes, including U.S. and EU measures. The Company also faces risks from short-term or costly content licenses, competing providers restricting access, unsuccessful or expensive in-house content, and the cost or unavailability of required digital-rights security solutions.

nodes.title: Workforce, Reseller, and Technology Risks
key_items: The Company’s success depends largely on the talents and efforts of its team members, the continued service and availability of highly skilled employees, including key personnel, and the Company’s ability to nurture its distinctive and inclusive culture.
The Company depends on the performance of carriers, wholesalers, retailers and other resellers.
The Company’s business and reputation are impacted by information technology system failures and network disruptions.
nodes.summary: The Company’s success relies on attracting and retaining skilled employees and key personnel amid intense competition and changing workforce dynamics, while preserving its distinctive, inclusive culture. It depends on carriers, wholesalers, retailers, and resellers, whose financing offers, financial health, distribution, and marketing may change; investments to support resellers may not generate returns. Technology and supply-chain systems face failures and disruptions from diverse causes, and continuity measures may prove inadequate, affecting online services, transactions, manufacturing, and shipping and harming business, reputation, results, and financial condition.

nodes.title: Losses or unauthorized access to or releases of confidential information, including personal information, could subject the Company to significant reputational, financial, legal and operational consequences.
nodes.summary: The Company faces significant risks from loss, disclosure, or unauthorized access to confidential and personal information, including through its own systems, employees, suppliers, and other third parties. Despite security measures, attacks are frequent, growing in sophistication, and may disrupt operations, harm customers and business relationships, affect stock value, or trigger litigation, investigations, fines, and other losses; the Company’s profile and valuable data make it a relatively attractive target. Controls and insurance may be inadequate, while protective measures can impede customer access or orders. New business investments and acquisitions may distract management, incur unexpected costs or liabilities, face regulatory obstacles, fail to deliver returns, or cause impairments and losses. Retail operations also face macroeconomic and other risks involving store costs, retail partners, inventory values, and obtaining or renewing desirable leases.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity, Investments, and Retail Risks
key_items: Investment in new business strategies and acquisitions could disrupt the Company’s ongoing business, present risks not originally contemplated and materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s retail stores are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties.
nodes.summary: The Company faces frequent, increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks that may disrupt operations, expose data, harm customers and business relationships, and lead to litigation, investigations, or financial penalties; its profile and valuable information increase targeting risk. Security measures and insurance may not prevent or cover all incidents, and protective actions can impede customer access or orders. New strategies and acquisitions may distract management, incur unexpected costs or liabilities, fail to deliver returns, or face regulatory obstacles, harming performance and reputation. Retail operations also face macroeconomic and other risks, including store costs, partner relationships, inventory-value changes, and securing affordable leases.

summary: The section covers risks to competitiveness and demand from product innovation, transitions, and market acceptance; outsourced manufacturing, logistics, component supply, quality, and inventory; intellectual property and digital content, software, and developer dependencies; workforce retention, resellers, and technology-system continuity; and cybersecurity, privacy, and information loss. It also addresses potential legal, regulatory, financial, operational, and reputational consequences, alongside risks from investments, acquisitions, and retail operations.

title: Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks
key_items: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition could be adversely impacted by unfavorable results of legal proceedings or government investigations.
The Company is subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide, which exposes the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

Expectations relating to environmental, social and governance considerations and related reporting obligations expose the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs, reputational harm, and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

The technology industry, including, in some instances, the Company, is subject to intense media, political and regulatory scrutiny, which exposes the Company to increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties.
The Company’s business is subject to a variety of U.S. and international laws, rules, policies and other obligations regarding data protection.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s legal and regulatory risks: growing litigation, investigations, patent claims and indemnification exposure can create substantial defense and settlement costs, damages, injunctions, operational changes, and reputational or financial harm; insurance may be inadequate. Complex, changing global laws across numerous areas may raise costs, constrain products, supply chains and business practices, or lead to penalties and import/export bans. ESG commitments and reporting create execution, compliance, liability and reputational risks. Technology-sector scrutiny and antitrust actions—including App Store, DMA, U.S. smartphone and search-partner matters—may prompt fines and business changes that affect users, competition, demand and revenue. Evolving privacy and data-protection rules, public privacy commitments, and special requirements for health, financial, biometric and payment-card data create compliance costs, investigations, liability, fines, higher transaction costs, or loss of card-processing capability.

title: Financial Risks
key_items: The Company expects its quarterly net sales and results of operations to fluctuate.
The Company’s financial performance is subject to risks associated with changes in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies.
The Company is exposed to credit risk and fluctuations in the values of its investment portfolio.

The Company is exposed to credit risk on its trade accounts receivable, vendor non-trade receivables and prepayments related to long-term supply agreements, and this risk is heightened during periods when economic conditions worsen.
The Company is subject to changes in tax rates, the adoption of new U.S. or international tax legislation and exposure to additional tax liabilities.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s financial risks: fluctuating quarterly sales and margins driven by seasonality, product concentration and demand, pricing, competition, costs, product launches, supply and operational disruptions; foreign-exchange effects and limits of hedging; investment-value and customer/vendor credit risks; and changing tax laws, rates, and audit liabilities. General risks include stock-price volatility and unmet market expectations for growth, dividends, or buybacks. It reports no unresolved staff comments and describes cybersecurity leadership, security and supplier-risk processes, incident escalation, enterprise-risk integration, and Audit Committee and Board oversight.

title: Risks, Stock Volatility, and Cybersecurity
key_items: The price of the Company’s stock is subject to volatility.
Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments; Item 1C. Cybersecurity
summary: The page notes uncertainty around tax examinations and potential adverse financial effects from higher tax rates or liabilities. It describes stock-price volatility and risks if growth, profitability, dividend, repurchase, or market expectations are unmet. Unresolved staff comments are listed as none. Cybersecurity responsibilities, security-team functions, supplier-risk and incident-management processes, enterprise-risk integration, and Audit Committee and Board oversight are outlined; related risks are referenced in Item 1A.

title: Company Properties and Legal Proceedings
key_items: Digital Markets Act Investigations; Department of Justice Lawsuit; Epic Games; Other Legal Proceedings
summary: The Company’s Cupertino headquarters and U.S. and international facilities support corporate, R&D, data, retail, and other operations and are considered suitable. Legal matters include EU Digital Markets Act investigations into App Store rules and iOS settings, with potential fines and immediate orders; a U.S. DOJ antitrust lawsuit and related claims; Epic Games litigation over external purchasing links and the Company’s compliance and injunction motions; and other routine proceedings, some settled without material impact. Adverse outcomes could materially affect results.

title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
summary: Item 4 reports that mine safety disclosures are not applicable. Item 5 states that Apple common stock trades on Nasdaq as AAPL and that it had 23,301 shareholders of record as of October 18, 2024. It reports 112.26 million shares repurchased from June 30 through September 28, 2024, at period-average prices of $224.11, $221.39 and $222.86. As of September 28, $20.9 billion of the $110 billion May 2024 authorization had been used, leaving $89.1 billion; Apple also used the remaining $4.1 billion from its 2023 program during the fourth quarter. Repurchases have no minimum requirement and may be made privately or on the open market, including through Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Listing, Holders, and Repurchases
key_items: Item 5. Market for Registrant’s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
Purchases of Equity Securities by the Issuer and Affiliated Purchasers
summary: Apple common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL, with 23,301 shareholders of record as of October 18, 2024. The page reports quarterly share repurchases by month, including shares purchased and average prices. As of September 28, 2024, $20.9 billion of the $110 billion May 2024 repurchase authorization had been used; Apple later completed the remaining $4.1 billion under its prior program. Repurchases have no minimum requirement and may occur through open-market or private transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Performance and Reserved Item 6
summary: A five-year, dividend-reinvested cumulative shareholder return comparison shows Apple, the S&P 500, and the Dow Jones U.S. Technology Supersector Index, each starting at $100 on September 27, 2019, with values reported through September 2024. The page cautions that past performance does not predict future results. Item 6 is reserved.

title: 2024 MD&A Context, Announcements and Fiscal Period
key_items: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
summary: The MD&A covers 2024 and 2023 comparisons, directing readers to the 2023 Form 10-K for 2022 and 2023–2022 discussion. Fiscal 2024 announcements included MacBook Pro and iMac, MacBook Air, iPad Air and Pro, operating-system updates, Apple Intelligence, iPhone 16 models, Apple Watch Series 10 and AirPods 4. Apple’s fiscal year ends on the last Saturday of September and spans 52 or 53 weeks; an extra week occurred in 2023, while 2024 and 2022 had 52 weeks. Inflation, interest rates and currency changes have affected and could materially affect results and financial condition.

title: Macroeconomic Conditions

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Conditions (intro)
nodes.summary: The MD&A should be read with the financial statements; it covers 2024–2023 comparisons, while 2022 discussion is in the prior 10-K. Fiscal 2024 announcements included new MacBook Pro and Air models, iMac, iPad Air and Pro, operating-system updates, Apple Intelligence, iPhone 16 models, Apple Watch Series 10 and AirPods 4. Fiscal years 2024 and 2022 had 52 weeks; 2023 had 53. Macroeconomic factors may affect results and financial condition. 2024 sales rose in the Americas, Europe, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific, but fell in Greater China; drivers included Services and iPhone, with currency weakness also reducing regional sales. Segment sales for 2022–2024 are reported.

nodes.title: 2024 Segment Operating Performance
nodes.summary: The page reports net sales by segment for 2024, 2023, and 2022, totaling $391.0 billion, $383.3 billion, and $394.3 billion, respectively. In 2024, sales rose in the Americas, Europe, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific, mainly due to Services growth in the Americas and Rest of Asia Pacific, Services and iPhone in Europe, and iPhone in Japan. Greater China sales fell due to lower iPhone and iPad sales. A weaker renminbi, yen, and other regional currencies versus the U.S. dollar adversely affected sales in their respective regions.

nodes.title: Rest of Asia Pacific
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2024, 2023 and 2022 net sales by geographic segment and product/service category. In 2024, total sales rose to $391.0 billion from $383.3 billion. Americas, Europe, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific increased, while Greater China declined; explanations cite product or Services sales changes and unfavorable currency effects in Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. By category, iPhone sales were relatively flat; Mac and Services increased; iPad and Wearables, Home and Accessories decreased. Services growth reflected advertising, App Store and cloud services. The tables also provide annual category and segment figures and year-over-year changes; Services includes amortization of deferred value for services bundled with certain products.

nodes.title: 2024 Product and Services Performance
nodes.summary: The page presents Apple net sales by category for 2024, 2023, and 2022, with year-over-year changes, and notes that Services sales include amortized value from services bundled with certain products. In 2024 versus 2023, iPhone sales were relatively flat; Mac sales rose, mainly from laptops; iPad sales fell due to lower iPad Pro and entry-level sales, partly offset by iPad Air growth; Wearables, Home and Accessories declined, mainly from Wearables and Accessories; and Services grew, mainly from advertising, the App Store, and cloud services.

nodes.title: Services
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2024–2022 net sales by product and service category, with comparisons and explanations: iPhone sales were flat in 2024; Mac rose on laptop sales; iPad fell due to lower Pro and entry-level sales, partly offset by iPad Air; Wearables, Home and Accessories declined; Services grew through advertising, the App Store and cloud services. It presents gross margins and percentages: product margins rose on cost savings, partly offset by mix and currency effects; Services margins rose due to sales and mix. Future margins face volatility and downward pressure. Operating expenses and sales percentages are reported: R&D increased mainly from headcount costs, while SG&A rose $1.2 billion.

nodes.title: Gross Margins and Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: The page reports Products, Services, and total gross margins and percentages for 2022–2024. In 2024, Products margin and percentage rose from 2023 due to cost savings, partly offset by product mix and currency weakness; Services margin rose mainly with higher sales, and its percentage rose with mix. Future gross margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expense figures and sales percentages are provided for R&D, SG&A, and total expenses across 2022–2024. 2024 R&D growth was driven mainly by headcount-related costs, while SG&A increased $1.2 billion.

summary: The section explains that the MD&A should be read alongside the financial statements, compares fiscal 2024 with 2023 (with 2022 discussion in the prior 10-K), notes fiscal-year week counts and key 2024 product and software announcements, and cautions that macroeconomic conditions affect results. It reports 2022–2024 sales by geography and product/service category, describing regional and category changes, currency effects, and growth drivers. It also presents gross margins and operating expenses and their sales percentages, explains 2024 margin and expense movements, and notes potential future margin volatility and downward pressure.

title: Operating Expenses
summary: The text reports Apple’s 2022–2024 product, services, and total gross margins and percentages. In 2024, product margin and percentage rose from 2023 due to cost savings, partly offset by product mix and currency weakness; services margin rose mainly on higher sales, and its percentage rose due to mix. Future gross margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expenses and sales percentages are provided: R&D growth reflected higher headcount costs, while selling, general and administrative expense rose $1.2 billion. Income-tax provisions and rates are listed; 2024’s higher effective rate reflected a $10.2 billion State Aid Decision charge and state taxes, partly offset by foreign-rate, R&D-credit, and share-based-compensation benefits. Versus 2023, the rate also rose due to higher foreign tax rates and lower share-based-compensation benefits.

title: Liquidity and Capital Resources
key_items: Debt; Leases; Manufacturing Purchase Obligations; Other Purchase Obligations; Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable
State Aid Decision Tax Payable; Capital Return Program
summary: The Company expects $140.8 billion in cash, operating cash flows and debt-market access to cover needs and capital returns. It details debt, interest, commercial paper, leases, manufacturing and other purchase obligations, and tax payables, including amounts due within 12 months. Its capital return program includes a $110 billion repurchase authorization, a $0.25 quarterly dividend and 2024 repurchases and dividends. It describes forthcoming income-tax and segment-reporting disclosure standards and critical estimates involving uncertain tax positions and legal contingencies, which could materially affect results.

title: Accounting Policies, Estimates, and Contingencies
key_items: Uncertain Tax Positions; Legal and Other Contingencies
summary: The page reports Apple’s €14.2 billion State Aid Decision payment obligation to Ireland, funded by escrow, and its capital return program, including 2024 repurchases and dividends. It describes forthcoming income-tax and segment-reporting disclosure standards and adoption dates. It explains how management develops critical accounting estimates, the judgment and potential financial effects involved in uncertain tax positions, and the treatment and possible impact of legal proceedings and other contingencies.

title: Market Risk: Interest Rates and Foreign Exchange
key_items: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
summary: Apple discusses exposure to interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks and strategies that may mitigate them. Rising U.S. rates can reduce investment portfolio fair value and increase term-debt interest expense; a 100-basis-point increase was estimated to affect these by $2.755 billion and $139 million in 2024, versus $3.089 billion and $194 million in 2023. A stronger U.S. dollar can harm sales and gross margins and affect asset and liability values. Mitigation may include derivatives, offsetting exposures, portfolio management, and local pricing, though some currency risks may remain unhedged. A Monte Carlo value-at-risk model estimated 95%-confidence maximum one-day derivative fair-value losses of $538 million in 2024 and $669 million in 2023; underlying exposures, excluded from the model, generally offset derivative fair-value changes.

title: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
summary: Item 8 indexes Apple’s consolidated financial statements: statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity, and cash flows for fiscal years 2024, 2023, and 2022; balance sheets for 2024 and 2023; notes; and independent auditor reports, with page references. Financial statement schedules are omitted because they are inapplicable, immaterial, or their required information is included in the statements and notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations for the fiscal years ended September 24, 2022, September 30, 2023, and September 28, 2024 report product and services net sales, cost of sales, gross margin, research and development and selling, general and administrative expenses, operating income, other income or expense, pretax income, income tax provision, and net income. They also present basic and diluted earnings per share and the corresponding weighted-average shares used in their calculation, in millions except shares (thousands) and per-share amounts, with accompanying notes referenced.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report net income, other comprehensive income or loss, and total comprehensive income for fiscal years ended September 28, 2024, September 30, 2023, and September 24, 2022. Other comprehensive items include foreign currency translation, unrealized gains or losses on derivative instruments, and unrealized gains or losses on marketable debt securities, including fair-value changes and adjustments for realized amounts. Figures are in millions, with accompanying financial statement notes referenced.

title: Apple Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets compare September 28, 2024, with September 30, 2023, in millions of dollars (shares in thousands, except par value). They list current and non-current assets, total assets, current and non-current liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and shareholders’ equity—including common stock, accumulated deficit, and accumulated other comprehensive loss—and reconcile total liabilities and equity to total assets. The statements refer readers to the accompanying notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY
summary: Apple’s consolidated shareholders’ equity statement reports beginning and ending equity balances for fiscal 2022–2024, with changes in common stock and additional paid-in capital (issuances, equity-award share withholding, and share-based compensation), retained earnings (net income, declared dividends, share withholding, and repurchases), and accumulated other comprehensive income or loss. Ending total equity was $50.672 billion in 2022, $62.146 billion in 2023, and $56.950 billion in 2024. Dividends declared per share or RSU were $0.90, $0.94, and $0.98, respectively; accompanying financial-statement notes are referenced.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents Apple’s consolidated cash flows for fiscal 2022–2024, including operating, investing, and financing activities; beginning and ending cash balances; changes in cash; and income taxes paid. It then summarizes accounting policies: consolidated entities, GAAP estimates and reclassifications, fiscal-year timing, revenue net of collected taxes, share-based compensation, cash equivalents, securities costing, inventory valuation, depreciation, derivative presentation, deferred taxes related to the TCJA minimum tax, and combining lease and nonlease components for certain facilities.

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated statements include its wholly owned subsidiaries, use GAAP-based management estimates, and reclassify certain prior-period amounts. Fiscal years end on the last Saturday of September and may include an extra week. Revenue excludes taxes collected for authorities; share-based compensation is recognized straight-line for awards expected to vest. Cash equivalents have purchase-date maturities of three months or less; securities sold use specific identification, and inventory uses FIFO. Property depreciation is straight-line. Derivatives are presented at gross fair value. Certain deferred taxes relate to the TCJA minimum tax on foreign earnings. Lease and nonlease components are combined for corporate, data center, and retail facility leases.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Revenue
nodes.summary: Revenue is recognized at expected consideration when control transfers—generally on shipment for products and over delivery for services—with prompt payment. Product sales are reduced for expected returns and incentives. Revenue for distinct obligations is allocated using relative observable or estimated stand-alone selling prices. iPhone, Mac and iPad sales include hardware/software recognized at shipment and bundled services deferred and recognized over their expected delivery period. Unbilled, undelivered long-term services are not recognized or disclosed. Third-party sales are reported gross when Apple controls the product; App Store application sales are reported net of commissions. The text provides 2022–2024 net sales by product and service, notes deferred-revenue recognition in each year and generally consistent segment sales mix except for a higher iPhone share in Greater China, and reports deferred revenue of $12.8 billion in 2024 versus $12.1 billion in 2023, with expected realization of 64% within one year, 25% in one to two years, 9% in two to three years, and 2% thereafter.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: Note 3 presents the basic and diluted earnings-per-share calculations for 2024, 2023, and 2022, including net income, weighted-average basic shares, dilutive share-based awards, diluted shares, and EPS. Net income was $93.736 billion, $96.995 billion, and $99.803 billion, respectively; basic EPS was $6.11, $6.16, and $6.15, and diluted EPS was $6.08, $6.13, and $6.11. About 24 million RSUs were excluded in 2023 because they were antidilutive. The text then begins Note 4, Financial Instruments.

nodes.title: Cash, Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities
nodes.summary: The tables detail Apple’s cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities by investment type and fair-value hierarchy at September 28, 2024 and September 30, 2023, including adjusted cost, unrealized gains and losses, fair value, and current/non-current classification. Level 2 valuations use quoted prices or models based on observable market data. Disclosures identify escrow-restricted cash and securities, report maturity distributions of 2024 non-current debt securities (excluding mortgage- and asset-backed securities) and mortgage-/asset-backed securities, and state that marketable debt investments are available-for-sale and classified current or non-current by maturity.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: The Company uses derivatives to partially manage foreign-exchange and interest-rate exposure, but may leave exposures unhedged due to accounting or cost considerations, and hedges may not fully offset losses. Derivative cash flows are classified with the hedged items, generally operating activities. Foreign-exchange hedging covers forecast revenue and inventory purchases (typically up to 12 months), foreign-currency term debt and securities (up to 18 years for term-debt cash flows), and certain remeasurement exposures; instruments may be designated cash-flow or fair-value hedges or remain undesignated. Interest-rate swaps, options, and other derivatives may hedge term debt or securities. The text reports derivative notional amounts for 2024 and 2023—designated foreign-exchange contracts of $64.069 billion and $74.730 billion, designated interest-rate contracts of $14.575 billion and $19.375 billion, and undesignated foreign-exchange contracts of $91.493 billion and $104.777 billion—and identifies marketable securities and term debt as items in fair-value hedges.

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable
nodes.summary: The text reports trade receivables and notes that cellular carriers represented 38% and 41% of balances in 2024 and 2023; certain customers provide credit support or collateral. Vendor non-trade receivables arise from component sales, with gains reducing product cost of sales when finished products are sold; two vendors represented 44% and 23% of balances in 2024 and 48% and 23% in 2023. It presents property and equipment by class, net balances, and depreciation expense for 2022–2024, plus details of other current and non-current assets and liabilities. It also describes the EU State Aid Decision, recovery amount, escrow balance and its balance-sheet classification.

nodes.title: Property, Plant, Equipment and Financial Statement Details
nodes.summary: Note 5 reports gross property, plant and equipment by asset class, accumulated depreciation and net totals for 2024 and 2023, plus depreciation expense for 2024, 2023 and 2022. Note 6 introduces consolidated financial statement details for 2024 and 2023, listing categories for other non-current assets, other current liabilities and other non-current liabilities, including income taxes payable. Note 7 begins Income Taxes.

nodes.title: European Commission State Aid Decision
nodes.summary: The European Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision found that Ireland had granted Apple improper tax benefits through 1991 and 2007 tax opinions and ordered recovery for June 2003–December 2014; Irish law ended their application from January 2015. The initial recovery was €13.1 billion plus €1.2 billion interest, later adjusted to €12.7 billion plus interest. At September 28, 2024, €14.2 billion ($15.8 billion), including investment gains, was held in restricted escrow. The General Court annulled the decision in 2020, but on September 10, 2024, the ECJ reversed that ruling and upheld the Commission. Apple recorded a fourth-quarter 2024 net tax charge of $10.2 billion, reflecting the $15.8 billion escrow release payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8 billion U.S. foreign tax credit and an $823 million reduction in unrecognized tax benefits.

nodes.title: Provision for Income Taxes and Effective Tax Rate
nodes.summary: Reports Apple’s income tax provision by federal, state, and foreign current/deferred taxes for 2022–2024, foreign pretax earnings, and a reconciliation to the 21% statutory rate, including state taxes, the State Aid Decision, foreign subsidiary earnings, R&D credits, equity-award tax benefits, and effective tax rates. It also details 2023–2024 deferred tax assets and liabilities, net deferred tax assets, indefinite Irish foreign tax and California R&D credit carryforwards, and valuation allowances.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: As of September 28, 2024, gross unrecognized tax benefits were $22.0 billion, including $10.8 billion that would affect the effective tax rate, up from $19.5 billion and $9.5 billion, respectively, in 2023. The text details 2022–2024 annual changes from prior- and current-year tax positions, settlements, and statute expirations. The Company files in U.S. federal, state, and foreign jurisdictions; certain years remain examinable. It expects benefits could decrease by $5–$13 billion over the next 12 months, mainly from transfer pricing and deemed repatriation tax matters.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 8 describes Apple’s equipment and facility leases, typically with terms up to 10 years and multiyear renewal options. It reports fixed and variable lease costs for 2022–2024, fixed operating-lease cash payments, and noncash ROU assets obtained for lease liabilities. It presents 2023 and 2024 operating and finance ROU assets and liabilities by balance-sheet line item, 2024 future lease-payment maturities and imputed interest, remaining lease terms and discount rates, and $849 million of fixed obligations for leases not yet commenced, expected to begin in 2025–2026.

nodes.title: Commercial Paper
nodes.summary: The Company issues unsecured commercial paper for short-term financing and uses proceeds for general corporate purposes, including dividends and share repurchases. Outstanding balances were $10.0 billion in 2024 and $6.0 billion in 2023, generally maturing in under nine months; weighted-average rates were 5.00% and 5.28%, respectively. A table reports net proceeds and repayments by maturity (90 days or less and over 90 days) and in total for 2024, 2023, and 2022.

nodes.title: Term Debt
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s term debt balances, maturities, effective interest rates, carrying-value adjustments, current and noncurrent portions, interest-rate and cross-currency hedging, and scheduled principal payments through 2029 and thereafter. It gives Notes’ fair values for 2024 and 2023. It also covers 2024 share repurchases, repurchase-program terms, and common-stock share changes for 2022–2024. Finally, it describes the 2022 and 2014 employee equity plans, their award types and terms, share authorization, and the 2014 Plan’s termination for new awards.

nodes.title: Share Repurchases, Common Stock and Employee Plans
nodes.summary: The page reports the fair value of the Company’s Notes at September 2024 and 2023. It describes 2024 repurchases of 499 million shares for $95.0 billion, noting programs have no minimum purchase requirement and allow negotiated or open-market transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans. A table lists common shares outstanding, repurchased and issued for 2022–2024. It also outlines the 2022 Employee Stock Plan’s award types, RSU vesting and dividend rights, and authorized shares, plus the 2014 Plan’s similar awards, cash bonuses and end of new-grant authority in 2022.

nodes.title: Equity Compensation and Purchase Commitments
nodes.summary: Reports RSU grants, vesting, cancellations, balances, and grant-date fair values for 2022–2024; vested RSU fair values, shares withheld for employee taxes, and related tax payments; share-based compensation expense and tax benefits for each year; and unrecognized RSU compensation cost and its expected recognition period. It also describes unconditional purchase obligations, their main sources, and future payment totals by period, including thereafter.

nodes.title: Legal Contingencies and Supply Concentrations
key_items: Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and Product
nodes.summary: The Company faces unresolved legal proceedings and claims from ordinary business, but management considers material losses—or losses exceeding recorded accruals—not reasonably possible. While most essential components have multiple sources, some rely on limited suppliers; industry competition, shortages, and commodity-price swings can affect availability and cost. Custom and new-technology components may have single sources and face initial capacity constraints, and suppliers may prioritize standard components. Most hardware is made by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Segment Information and Geographic Data
nodes.summary: Apple manages five geographic segments—Americas, Europe (including India, the Middle East and Africa), Greater China (mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan), Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific—according to customer and distribution-partner locations and regional market conditions. Segment performance is measured by net sales and operating income; assets are excluded from information reviewed by the chief operating decision maker. The text reports each segment’s sales and operating income for 2022–2024, reconciles segment operating income to consolidated operating income through R&D and other corporate expenses, and presents net sales for the U.S., China and other countries for 2022–2024, plus long-lived assets in those categories for 2023–2024.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Opinion on the Financial Statements; Basis for Opinion; Critical Audit Matter
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young LLP gives an unqualified opinion that Apple’s 2024 and 2023 consolidated balance sheets and three-year financial statements comply fairly, in all material respects, with U.S. GAAP; it also reports an unqualified opinion on internal controls. The report explains management’s and auditors’ responsibilities and PCAOB audit procedures. It identifies uncertain tax positions as a critical audit matter: $22.0 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits, including $10.8 billion affecting the effective tax rate. Audit work tested controls, assessed management’s judgments and supporting evidence, consulted tax specialists and external advisors, and reviewed disclosures. EY has served as auditor since 2009; report dated November 1, 2024.

The section concludes with the independent auditor’s unqualified opinions on the financial statements and internal controls, including its discussion of uncertain tax positions as a critical audit matter.

nodes.summary: No fourth-quarter 2024 changes materially affected, or were likely to materially affect, Apple’s internal financial reporting controls. Two executives adopted Rule 10b5-1 trading plans in August 2024: Deirdre O’Brien’s covers specified vesting shares through October 2026 and expires December 31, 2026; Jeff Williams’s covers up to 100,000 shares and specified vesting shares through October 2025 and expires December 15, 2025. It summarizes voting thresholds and rules for director elections, removal and vacancies, amendments, and meeting adjournments; discretionary dividends; pro rata liquidation distributions; and the absence of preemptive, conversion, redemption, or sinking-fund rights. nodes.title: The Notes
key_items: The 0.000% 2025 Notes; The 0.875% 2025 Notes; The 2026 Notes; The 2027 Notes; The 1.375% 2029 Notes
The 3.050% 2029 Notes; The 2031 Notes; The 2042 Notes
nodes.summary: The summary describes Apple’s Notes, governed by New York law under its 2013 and 2018 Indentures, whose full terms control. The Indentures allow unlimited debt issuance and additional similar securities without existing holders’ consent, subject to ISIN conditions. As of October 18, 2024, outstanding Notes comprised euro-denominated 2025 (0% and 0.875%), 2026 (1.625%), 2027 (2%), 2029 (1.375%), and 2031 (0.5%) issues, plus sterling-denominated 2029 (3.05%) and 2042 (3.6%) issues. The text gives each issue’s original principal and issuance date, maturity, coupon, payment frequency and dates, and outstanding principal.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: The Notes rank equally with the issuer’s other senior unsecured, unsubordinated debt, but are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and preferred stock and effectively subordinated to secured debt up to the value of its collateral. Subsidiary creditors, including trade creditors and preferred stockholders, generally have priority over Noteholders in subsidiary assets and earnings. The Indentures do not limit the issuer or its subsidiaries from incurring additional debt.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: The euro-denominated 0.000% and 0.875% 2025, 2026, 2027, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes switch to U.S.-dollar payments if euros become unavailable or cease to be used as specified; the 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes are payable in pounds sterling, or euros if the UK adopts the euro, and similarly switch to dollars if that currency becomes unavailable or, for euros, ceases to be used. Dollar amounts use the Federal Reserve’s mandated exchange rate or, absent one, the latest Wall Street Journal rate from on or before the second Business Day before payment. Such dollar payments are not defaults. Business Day definitions differ: the euro notes require New York and London banks to be open and TARGET2 operating; the sterling/euro notes exclude bank-closing days in New York, London, or the payment location.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: Notes generally require principal and interest payments free of U.S. tax withholding unless legally required. The Company must pay non-U.S. holders additional amounts to preserve the stated net payment, subject to exceptions for U.S.-connected holders, intermediaries or beneficial owners who would not qualify, missing tax certifications, non-withholding taxes, late law changes or presentation, specified taxes, alternative paying-agent arrangements, FATCA-related taxes, and combinations of these exceptions. The Notes remain subject to applicable tax laws; no other tax payments are required. The text defines “United States” and “United States person” for these provisions and tax redemptions.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: If specified post-prospectus changes to U.S. tax laws, regulations, rulings, or their official interpretation cause or are expected (based on independent counsel’s opinion) to cause additional amounts to be payable on a Notes series, the issuer may redeem that series in whole, but not in part. Notice periods vary by series: 30–60 days for the 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029, and 2042 Notes; 15–60 days for the 0.875% 2025 and 1.375% 2029 Notes; and 10–60 days for the 0.000% 2025 and 2031 Notes. Redemption is at 100% of principal plus accrued, unpaid interest, with interest excluded through the redemption date for the latter two series.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The text sets out optional redemption terms for several note series. The 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes may be redeemed at any time at the greater of par or the discounted present value of remaining payments plus series-specific spreads. The 0.000% and 0.875% 2025, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes have similar make-whole pricing before their specified Par Call Dates, but redeem at par on or afterward. Accrued interest is paid to redemption; scheduled interest remains payable to record-date holders. It defines Par Call Dates, the applicable German or UK government-bond benchmarks, and the Comparable Government Bond Rate calculation.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indentures contain limited covenants and do not cap debt or lease obligations, restrict debt secured by liens, or limit dividends, distributions, or stock repurchases/redemptions. They permit mergers, consolidations, and transfers of substantially all assets if the successor is appropriately organized in the U.S., assumes the obligations and conversion rights, and no default exists; under the 2013 Indenture, the trustee must also receive an officers’ certificate and counsel’s opinion. The successor replaces the issuer, gains its rights and powers, and releases it from related obligations. “Person” is broadly defined to include individuals, entities, governments, and their subdivisions or agencies.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: Events of default include overdue interest (30 days), unpaid principal or premium, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ notice, specified voluntary or court-ordered bankruptcy events, and other series-specific defaults. The text defines Bankruptcy Law and Custodian and explains acceleration, automatic acceleration for bankruptcy defaults, and rescission by majority holders after required deposits and cure or waiver. Defaults are series-specific. It also covers annual officer certifications, holder conditions for bringing proceedings, majority holders’ control of remedies and ability to waive defaults, trustee duties and indemnity protections, and each holder’s unconditional right to payment and suit.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: Indenture amendments generally require approval by holders of a majority of the affected series, while changes to core payment, redemption, enforcement, voting, waiver, and conversion rights require each affected holder’s consent. The company and trustee may make specified changes without holder consent, including adding protections, defaults, guarantees, security, trustees, or securities; addressing succession, issuance, form, documentation, and legal or market rules; and making nonmaterial or series-limited changes, corrections, or defeasance provisions. A series majority may waive certain covenants and past defaults, except payment defaults or provisions requiring unanimous consent; a waiver cures only the specific default and does not affect later defaults or related rights.

nodes.title: Discharge, Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The indentures permit discharge of near-term or matured Notes by depositing sufficient U.S. dollars with the trustee, which may be invested in short-term U.S. Treasury securities or eligible money-market funds. Issuers may also choose legal defeasance, ending most obligations while retaining specified administrative and payment duties, or covenant defeasance, releasing restrictive-covenant obligations and certain defaults. Both require an irrevocable, sufficient deposit of dollars and/or qualifying government obligations; after covenant defeasance, the issuer remains liable if funds do not cover accelerated payments. German obligations qualify for specified 2025–2031 Notes, and UK obligations for the 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes. A tax opinion is required; legal defeasance additionally requires an IRS ruling or change in law. Legal defeasance remains available after covenant defeasance.

nodes.title: Book-Entry Settlement and Certificated Notes
nodes.summary: The Notes are issued as global book-entry securities deposited with a common depositary for Euroclear and Clearstream, and beneficial interests generally cannot be exchanged for certificates. Subject to specified conditions, global Notes may be exchanged for definitive certificated Notes in stated euro or sterling denominations if the depositary cannot continue and no successor is appointed within 90 days, the issuer elects to end global representation, or a continuing event of default occurs. Certificates are issued in authorized denominations and registered as directed by the depositary; otherwise, global Notes may only be replaced by equivalent global Notes.

nodes.title: The Trustee for the Notes
nodes.summary: The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, N.A. serves as trustee under the Indentures. The issuer has commercial deposit and custodial arrangements with BNYM and its affiliates, may establish further banking relationships with them, and BNYM also serves as trustee and paying agent for the issuer’s other debt securities and may do so for future issuances.

It covers optional make-whole and par redemption, limited covenants and successor transactions, defaults and enforcement, amendments and waivers, discharge and defeasance, global book-entry settlement and conditions for certificated Notes, and the trustee’s role and banking relationships.

summary: Apple Inc.’s 2022 Employee Stock Plan restricted stock unit award notice records participant and grant details, including employee ID, grant number, units, award date, vesting commencement date, and vesting schedule. The award is governed by the Plan and incorporated RSU terms. Participation is optional: the recipient may promptly decline by emailing Apple’s Stock Plan Group; otherwise, it is deemed accepted unless declined by the last day of the month before the first vesting date.

title: TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF RESTRICTED STOCK UNIT AWARD

nodes.title: TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF RESTRICTED STOCK UNIT AWARD (intro)
nodes.summary: The agreement governs discretionary Apple 2022 Plan RSU awards, alongside each Grant Notice, and defines the participant and award date. RSUs are nonvoting bookkeeping units representing a potential right to shares, not property or a trust. Awards vest according to the Grant Notice, subject to specified conditions; fractional units carry forward toward a whole share or may be forfeited at termination. Vesting generally requires active service through each vesting date; approved nonpersonal leave counts, while personal leave counts for 30 days before vesting pauses. The award guarantees neither employment nor continued service and does not limit termination or changes to other compensation, while preserving independent contractual rights absent consent.

nodes.title: 5. Dividend and Voting Rights.
nodes.summary: The text sets out terms for Apple 2022 Employee Stock Plan RSU awards, including a performance-award notice, acceptance deadline, discretionary and unsecured award status, vesting and continued-service requirements, and leave rules. It covers limited shareholder rights and dividend equivalents, transfer restrictions, settlement and tax withholding, termination treatment for disability or death, clawbacks, stock adjustments, data privacy and electronic delivery, notices, Plan incorporation, agreement amendments, unsecured-creditor status, governing law and venue, 409A intent, severability, and additional Company requirements. Performance awards’ dividend equivalents track target RSUs and vesting outcomes.

nodes.title: 7. Timing and Manner of Settlement of RSUs.
nodes.summary: Vested RSUs will be settled by delivering the corresponding Shares, less Tax-Related Items, on or as soon as administratively practicable after the applicable Vesting Date and no later than 2½ months afterward. Delivery is conditional on the recipient providing any representations, documents, or assurances required under Plan Section 13(c). The Participant has no further rights to RSUs once settled or forfeited under Section 8.

nodes.title: 8. Effect of Termination of Service.
nodes.summary: Unvested RSUs and related dividend equivalents generally terminate on the participant’s last day of employment or service, regardless of the reason. If termination is due to death or disability before vesting, a prorated amount may vest on the scheduled date, subject to performance conditions; remaining units are canceled without payment. The award and related proceeds are subject to applicable legal and company clawbacks. The company may demand repayment for specified felonies, confidentiality or insider-information breaches, theft, embezzlement, fraud, or material contract breaches, and may instruct brokers or administrators to return assets. Participants must comply; company clawback policies prevail in conflicts, and these remedies are nonexclusive.

nodes.title: 10. Adjustments Upon Specified Events.
nodes.summary: The Committee adjusts outstanding RSUs and the number or type of securities deliverable for specified stock events under Plan Section 11, but not ordinary cash dividends covered by dividend equivalent rights. The Participant remains ultimately responsible for all related taxes; the Company and Employer make no tax-treatment assurances or tax-planning commitments, and multiple jurisdictions may require withholding. Before the relevant tax event, the Participant must pay or arrange satisfactory payment and authorizes withholding from compensation, shares or dividend equivalents, share-sale proceeds, or other permitted methods. Section 16 officers are generally subject to share or dividend-equivalent withholding unless the Board or Committee selects another authorized method. Withholding may use statutory or maximum rates; excess may be refunded in cash or claimed from tax authorities, while shortfalls remain payable. Shares withheld for taxes count as issued, and delivery may be withheld if the Participant does not meet tax obligations.

nodes.title: 12. Electronic Delivery and Acceptance.
nodes.summary: The agreement covers electronic delivery and online participation consent; collection, use, and worldwide transfer of participant data for plan administration; written notice procedures; incorporation of and compliance with the Plan, including limits on discretionary rights; the entire agreement, written amendments, and limited unilateral waivers; the participant’s status as an unsecured creditor with no trust or asset interest; headings; California and federal governing law and exclusive California venue; interpretation to avoid Section 409A tax; severability; and the Company’s right to impose additional requirements and obtain related agreements.

nodes.summary: The notice provides fields for participant, employee ID, grant number, unit amount, award and vesting dates, and vesting schedule. nodes.title: Apple 2022 RSU Award Terms

title: Insider Trading Policy and Coverage
key_items: This policy is designed to prevent trading of securities when a person is aware of material nonpublic information.
Who is Covered by this Policy?
summary: The policy aims to prevent securities trading while aware of material nonpublic information. Insider trading is a crime that can bring fines, damages, and imprisonment; U.S. and international authorities actively monitor, investigate, and prosecute even small violations regardless of motive, trade size, or profit. The policy covers Apple personnel, specified family members, and any person or entity whose securities trading they influence or control, and requires them to ensure those parties comply.

title: Insider Trading Prohibitions
summary: Apple prohibits trading its securities while aware of material nonpublic information, tipping or recommending trades based on it, trading or tipping about other companies using work-related inside information, and trading during restricted periods. Short sales, hedging, derivatives, and (for directors and executive officers) pledging Apple stock are barred. Materiality depends on context and may involve positive or negative information; information generally remains nonpublic for 24 hours after effective public release, while rumors do not count. Violations may lead to discipline, termination, equity-award repayment, and civil or criminal penalties. Personnel with questions should contact Apple’s team.

title: Insider Information and Policy Violations
summary: Explains that materiality depends on all relevant circumstances, investor importance, and potential price impact; positive or negative information may be material, and standards vary by company. Nonpublic information is not available to the public and remains so for at least 24 hours after an official public release; rumors do not count as effective distribution. Violations may result in discipline, termination, equity-award repayment, and civil or criminal penalties. Personnel with questions or doubts should contact Apple’s team.

title: Restricted Trading Periods and Trading Windows
summary: Apple personnel, covered family members, and entities notified by Corporate Legal may not trade during restricted periods. Trading windows permit trades only when the individual lacks material nonpublic information; this prohibition applies even outside restricted periods. Quarterly restrictions begin December 1, March 1, June 1, and September 1, and end 24 hours after public disclosure of the respective quarterly or year-end results (typically early February, May, August, or November). Apple may impose or extend special restrictions; notified individuals must not discuss them.

title: Permitted Transactions
summary: The policy exempts certain transactions from its restrictions, even during restricted periods or open trading windows: vesting of restricted stock units and Apple withholding shares for taxes; purchases through Apple’s Employee Stock Purchase Plan; cash-settled equity-plan option exercises; trades under an Apple-acknowledged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan; and bona fide estate-planning gifts, if the employee or immediate family remain sole beneficiaries and the shares retain the policy’s restrictions. Other securities gifts remain subject to the policy, including restricted-period trading prohibitions and designated-individual pre-clearance requirements.

title: Additional Information Regarding Section 16 and Designated Individuals
summary: Apple’s General Counsel and authorized delegates act as Insider Trading Compliance Officers. Designated Individuals include directors, executives, certain designated people, and their covered family members and entities; Apple Legal notifies those affected. Except for permitted transactions, they must request pre-clearance at least two business days in advance, trade only during the notice’s validity, and disclose relevant circumstances while ensuring they have no material nonpublic information. Compliance Officers need another officer’s pre-clearance to trade. Section 16 reporting persons must also meet statutory reporting duties and short-swing profit restrictions.

title: Rule 10b5-1 Trading Plans
summary: Rule 10b5-1 plans are exempt from the policy’s trading restrictions only if preapproved by Apple Legal and meet requirements: applicable cooling-off periods (Section 16 persons: later of 90 days after adoption/modification or two business days after the relevant 10-K/10-Q filing, capped at 120 days; others: later of 30 days after execution or 24 hours after the quarter’s earnings announcement), good faith, no awareness of material nonpublic information (MNPI), predetermined transaction terms, no subsequent influence, unaltered execution, and no related hedging. Section 16 plans must include specified representations. Apple’s compliance officer may impose conditions; only one plan is generally allowed, subject to limited Rule 10b5-1 exceptions and preapproval. Plans may be modified only during an open window without MNPI; modifications and terminations require Legal preapproval, and changes to amount, price, or timing restart the cooling-off period. The plan initiator is responsible for compliance and execution.

key_items: E. Rights and Remedies; Waiver; Amendment; Extension
summary: Apple’s Rule 10D-1 Recovery Policy, administered by its People and Compensation Committee, applies to executive officers who served during the performance period for covered incentive compensation received on or after October 2, 2023. Covered compensation is tied wholly or partly to financial-reporting measures, including stock price and shareholder return; time-based awards are excluded, though other Apple policies may cover them. The Committee oversees administration, disclosures, records, and binding determinations. Following a qualifying accounting restatement, Apple must make reasonable efforts to recover excess gross pre-tax compensation received in the preceding three fiscal years and any applicable short transition period, using reasonable estimates for stock-based awards. Recovery may be excused under specified Rule 10D-1 conditions after considering shareholders’ interests. The Committee chooses prompt recovery methods; Apple will not indemnify executives. The policy supplements other remedies, prevents duplicate recovery unless legally required, and may be waived, amended, or extended.
